lead: Liquid extraction pulls a dissolved solute out of one liquid by contacting it with a second liquid; leaching does the same job on a solid. This unit goes from the ternary diagram and single-stage balances to cross-current and counter-current cascades, the contactors that carry them out, and the percolation, moving-bed and Shanks routes used for oilseeds, sugar and ores. After it you can count ideal stages for an extraction or leaching battery, size a mixer-settler or column, and choose equipment for a duty.
about: The unit starts with the solvent and the triangular diagram (5.1): what makes a good solvent, how a mixture point splits along a tie line, and the lever rule. Chapter 5.2 repeats the stage with fresh solvent (cross-current) and 5.3 turns the solvent round (counter-current), counting stages with the difference point on the right-angled diagram or with the Kremser equation; only a few universities teach that construction in detail. Chapter 5.4 sizes the hardware: mixer-settlers and spray, packed and agitated columns. Chapter 5.5 moves to solids, with the inert-solid balance, leaching equipment and cross-current leaching, and 5.7 extends it to percolation, moving beds, the Shanks system and counter-current batteries. Chapter 5.6 covers pulsed, centrifugal and supercritical extraction.

chapters.idea: A solvent that dissolves the solute but not the carrier splits a liquid mixture into two layers, and the ternary diagram predicts how the solute divides between them.
chapters.depth: Solvent selection: selectivity, distribution coefficient well away from 1, density difference for settling, interfacial tension, low mutual solubility, low viscosity, easy recovery of solute from solvent, cost, toxicity, flammability. Define solute (A), carrier or diluent (B), solvent (S), extract, raffinate. Teach the equilateral triangular diagram: axes in mass or mole fraction, reading a point and its perpendiculars, the binodal (solubility) curve, single-phase and two-phase regions, tie lines, plait point, and conversion to solute-free mass ratios X and Y. Distribution coefficient K = y/x on a mass-fraction basis; how K varies with composition and temperature. Name the three types of ternary system by how many pairs are partially miscible, and note that some syllabi call the plot a Gibbs triangle.

figure.aria: Two liquid layers, each holding solute, with the shared part being the solute that has distributed between them at equilibrium.

chapters.example: 100 kg/h of a feed containing 30 mass% acetic acid in water is contacted with 100 kg/h of pure ether in one stage. Neglect the mutual solubility of water and ether. At equilibrium the water-rich layer contains 10 mass% acid and the ether-rich layer contains 20 mass%. Find the mass of each layer, the acid recovered and the percentage recovery.
chapters.trap: Tie lines are only horizontal on a right-angled plot with the solute on the vertical axis; on the equilateral triangle they follow the binodal curve, so points read off by eye go wrong.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: equilibrium stage, stage efficiency, and the meaning of a distribution coefficient.
chapters.leave: Stage-to-stage balances to 5.2 and 5.3; contactor hardware to 5.4.

chapters.idea: One equilibrium stage gives one split; repeating the contact with fresh solvent on the leftover raffinate gives a geometric drop in solute, which can be summed in a single formula.
chapters.depth: Single-stage mass balance with and without mutual solubility; the graphical construction on the triangle, where the mixture point lies on the line joining feed and solvent and the tie line through it gives both phase compositions. Cross-current cascade: feed flows stage to stage, fresh solvent enters every stage. Constant-K case, with X_n = X_0/(1 + K·S/R)^n where X is kg solute per kg carrier, S is kg pure solvent per stage, R is kg carrier in the feed, K is the mass-ratio distribution coefficient and n the number of stages. Solvent split between stages versus all in one stage; stage efficiency; batch extraction in a single vessel.

figure.title: Three-stage cross-current train
figure.aria: Feed passes from stage 1 to stage 3 while a separate stream of fresh solvent enters every stage, so each contact starts with clean solvent.

chapters.example: 500 kg of a solution containing 125 kg solute and 375 kg carrier is extracted in three cross-current stages, each using 200 kg of pure solvent. The distribution coefficient is constant at K = 2.0 on a solute-free mass-ratio basis (Y = 2X). Find the solute left in the final raffinate and the percentage recovered.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the two schemes: putting all 600 kg of solvent into one stage gives a very different answer from splitting it into three 200 kg portions, so read which one the question asks.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1: ternary equilibrium, tie lines and K.
chapters.leave: Counter-current flow and the graphical stage count to 5.3; sizing of mixers and settlers to 5.4.

chapters.idea: Running solvent against the feed instead of adding it fresh at every stage makes each stage meet a richer solvent, so the same recovery needs fewer stages and less solvent.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the graphical right-angle construction in detail; others want only the Kremser equation. Cover the counter-current cascade, overall and stage-to-stage balances, the operating line joining (X_0, Y_1) to (X_N, Y_{N+1}), the right-angled (Hunter-Nash) construction of stages between the operating line and the equilibrium curve, and the pinch that fixes the minimum solvent rate. Constant-K case with extraction factor E = K·S/R and X_N = X_0(E - 1)/(E^(N+1) - 1) for E not equal to 1, with symbols as in 5.2. Compare stage counts and solvent use against cross-current at the same duty.

figure.title: Counter-current stages on the right-angle diagram
figure.aria: The operating line lies below the equilibrium curve; each pair of stage points marks where a stage steps between the two lines, and three steps take the raffinate from the feed composition to the final one.

chapters.example: 700 kg/h of carrier carrying 300 kg/h of solute (X_0 = 0.4286) is extracted counter-currently with 500 kg/h of pure solvent in three stages. Take Y = 1.5X. Find the solute left in the raffinate, the loading of the extract leaving stage 1, and the percentage recovery.
chapters.trap: The operating line is not the equilibrium line: it runs from the feed point on the left to the entering solvent point on the right, and drawing it the other way round silently reverses the whole cascade.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.1 and 5.2; Unit 2 for the idea of an operating line.
chapters.leave: Multistage leaching, which reuses the same algebra, to 5.7; column design to 5.4.

chapters.idea: Every extractor must mix the two liquids to make interfacial area and then let them settle apart, and each equipment type is a different answer to those two jobs.
chapters.depth: Mixer-settler: mixer volume gives residence time, settler area is sized on the dispersed-phase flow divided by the settling velocity, stage efficiency as approach to equilibrium, number of units taken from the stage count. Spray column, packed column and mechanically agitated contactors: which phase to disperse, drop size, hold-up, flooding, axial mixing, and HTU-NTU design for a packed extractor, in the same spirit as Unit 3. Rotating-disc and reciprocating-plate contactors named only, since 5.6 covers pulsed units. Selection table on capacity, stages per unit height, floor space and solvent inventory.

figure.title: One mixer-settler stage
figure.aria: Feed and solvent join in the mixer, the mixed stream goes to the settler, and the settler sends out two separate streams, the extract and the raffinate.

chapters.example: A mixer-settler stage handles 2 m³/h of combined feed and solvent. The mixer holds 0.5 m³. The dispersed phase flow is 1 m³/h and its drops settle at 0.6 m/h. Find the mixing time and the settler area required.
chapters.trap: Sizing the settler on the total flow instead of the dispersed-phase flow, and quoting stage efficiency as if it were the number of stages.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.1 to 5.3; Unit 2 for stage efficiency and interphase transfer; Unit 3 for HTU and flooding ideas.
chapters.leave: Pulsed, centrifugal and supercritical machines to 5.6.

chapters.idea: In leaching the solvent must soak into a solid, dissolve the solute and diffuse back out, and the spent solid always carries some solution away with it, so the balance is written on an inert-solid basis.
chapters.depth: Solid-liquid equilibrium and the assumption of equilibrium between the solution inside the solid and the bulk solution. Inert (insoluble solid) basis: r = kg solution retained per kg inert solid, X = kg solute per kg solution, overflow and underflow streams. Single-stage and cross-current leaching balances with constant r; stage efficiency. Equipment: batch agitated vessel, Pachuca tank, Dorr agitator and thickener, continuous counter-current decantation, and named continuous units. Keep the numerical work to one or two stages here.

figure.title: One leaching stage
figure.aria: Solid feed and solvent enter the leacher, and two streams leave: a strong solution overflow and a spent solid underflow still carrying retained solution.

chapters.example: 1000 kg of a solid containing 20 mass% oil and 80 mass% inert material is leached in one stage with 500 kg of pure solvent. The spent solid retains 0.5 kg of solution per kg of inert solid. Find the oil recovered in the overflow and the percentage recovery.
chapters.trap: Balancing on total solid mass instead of inert mass, and forgetting that the underflow leaves with solution in it, which is where most of the lost solute hides.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1 for the idea of a distribution between two phases; Unit 2 for equilibrium stages.
chapters.leave: Percolation, moving beds, the Shanks system and long counter-current trains to 5.7.

chapters.idea: When a plain column is too slow or too tall, you add pulsation to stir the phases, spin them in a centrifugal field to settle them fast, or replace the liquid solvent with a supercritical fluid whose dissolving power is set by pressure.
chapters.depth: Pulsed columns: sieve plates or packing with a reciprocating pulse, pulse velocity = 2 × amplitude × frequency, effect on drop breakup, hold-up and throughput, and the extra height needed for the pulse. Centrifugal extractors: Podbielniak and mixer-settler centrifuges, short residence time, small hold-up, use for heat-sensitive or radioactive systems. Supercritical extraction: critical point of CO2 at 31.1 °C and 73.8 bar, density and solvent power rising with pressure at fixed temperature, selectivity, easy solvent removal, applications such as decaffeination and natural-product extraction. Keep each machine short; the emphasis is on why it exists.

figure.title: Three ways to intensify extraction
figure.aria: The same feed and solvent can be sent through a pulsed column, a centrifugal extractor or a supercritical CO2 contactor, and all three deliver an extract and a raffinate.

chapters.example: 2 kg of ground spice containing 5 mass% essential oil is extracted with supercritical CO2 at 40 °C and 200 bar. The CO2 leaves the bed loaded with 1.5 mass% oil. Find the minimum mass of CO2 needed and the extraction time at a CO2 flow of 5 kg/h.
chapters.trap: Thinking a supercritical fluid is a gas with no solvent power: above the critical point the density can be liquid-like, and it is the pressure, not the temperature alone, that changes what dissolves.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.4 for column behaviour, flooding and dispersed-phase choice.
chapters.leave: Detailed mechanical design of the machines; the thermodynamics of supercritical fluids belongs to a thermodynamics course.

chapters.idea: Solvent can be pushed through a stationary bed, run against slowly moving solids, or recycled through a battery of tanks in the Shanks system, and all of these are costed with the same multistage leaching balance.
chapters.depth: Percolation through a stationary bed: diffusion from inside the particle versus simple washing of the surface, why the first runnings are strong, and how the bed is drained and re-flooded. Moving-bed leaching and named continuous units. The Shanks system: tanks in a row, solids moving one way, liquor the other, fresh wash water entering at the last tank and strong liquor drawn from the first; liquor advance and wash ratio; number of tanks for a target recovery. Multistage cross-current and counter-current leaching with constant retention r, and the counter-current formula X_N/X_0 = (E - 1)/(E^(N+1) - 1) with E = V/L, V the overflow solution rate and L = r·B the retained solution rate, B being the inert solid rate. Stage efficiency.

figure.title: Shanks battery, four tanks
figure.aria: Solids move from tank 1 to tank 4 while fresh wash water enters at tank 4 and moves the other way, so the strongest liquor leaves tank 1.

chapters.example: 1000 kg/h of a solid containing 25 mass% solute and 75 mass% inert is leached in a three-stage counter-current train. Fresh water enters at 600 kg/h and the spent solid retains 0.6 kg of solution per kg of inert solid. Find the solute lost with the spent solid and the percentage recovery.
chapters.trap: Running the solids and the liquor the same way: if both move left to right the train is cross-current in disguise and the wash water leaves loaded instead of the product liquor.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.5 for the inert-solid basis and retention; Chapter 5.3 for the counter-current stage formula.
chapters.leave: Drying of the spent solid to Unit 7; the choice of solvent to Chapter 5.1.

links: tie lines and the lever rule give each stage
fresh solvent per stage becomes counter-current flow
faster contact: pulsing, centrifuges, supercritical CO₂
the inert-solid balance carries over to batteries
the Kremser form is reused for leaching
